title: GPU runtime profiling - kernel selection / TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM / CUDA graphs - deep dive with ZenithAI

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): ok everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a deep dive today on the gpu runtime profiling stuff, kernel selection, t n r t - uh tenso r t l l m vs v l l m, and cuda graphs and how that impacts steady-state latency and cost.
[00:12] Sofia (ZenithAI): thanks Maya, im excited. we saw some weird tail latency spikes when seq len changed, and our kv cache behavior seems off when we mix short and long contexts.
[00:27] Arjun (Redwood-SE): yeah so just to set context, we profiled a 7B model on A100s and 4090s in our dev cluster; the kernel selector in our runtime picks kernels based on block sizes, seq len distribution, and quantization mode. one of the gotchas is cuD A graph warmup interacting with dynamic kv cache sizes.
[00:45] Ethan (ZenithAI): sorry cuD A? you mean cuda graphs?
[00:48] Arjun: yes, sorry, cuda graphs. the transcription sometimes says coda.
[00:54] Priya (ZenithAI): we are on-prem, so we have mixed gen GPUs, DGX-ish machines and also some older 40-series. we care about predictability more than absolute best throughput.
[01:10] Maya: got it. quick question — are you trying to use TensorRT-LLM path or vLLM/integrated CPU path? or a mix?
[01:20] Sofia: we tried an experiment with TRT-LLM for int8 on a subset and vLLM for the rest. TRT gave better tokens/sec but we saw a quality regression for some prompts and weird latency when we spilled from cache.
[01:38] Arjun: that's common. TRT-LLM's kernel selection aggressively fuses ops and uses specialized attention kernels, which improves throughput but makes fallback and dynamic shapes harder. vLLM (the v l l m path) tends to be more flexible for kv cache reuse and variable batch sizes but isn't as optimized for int8 fused GEMMs.
[01:58] Sofia: can you explain the kernel selection heuristics? how do you pick between fused attention vs multi-head matmul kernels?
[02:10] Arjun: sure — high level: our selector considers model block size, head size, token length distribution, and target throughput vs latency SLO. for small sequence lengths (<128) we prefer tiled matmul kernels and smaller attention kernels; for long sequences or heavy kv reuse, we pick fused attention that reduces memory bandwidth. there are cost heuristics: cost_per_token = kernel_time + mem_copy + kv_cache_overhead. the selector learns from microbenchmarks per-machine.
[02:45] Ethan: you mentioned kv cache overhead — what is that exactly?
[02:49] Luis (Redwood): kv cache overhead includes the memcpy overhead to GPU memory, the pointer arithmetic for slice operations, and any reallocation if the cache grows beyond pre-allocated buffers. On mixed seq loads, you can get fragmentation and extra memcpy which increases p50/p95.
[03:10] Priya: that's what we see — our p95 jumps when a 1024 token job hits the system, even if most other requests are 64 tokens.
[03:18] Arjun: two quick mitigations: pre-allocate kv cache pools sized to 95th percentile sequence length, and use prefix caching (we perform prefix reuse and store compiled kernels keyed by prefix length). note that compiling many kernel variants increases binary size and warmup time.
[03:39] Sofia: how does CUDA graphs help? we heard it lowers cpu overhead but warmup is problematic.
[03:45] Arjun: CUDA graphs freeze the GPU work submission into a graph which removes CPU launch overhead and stream syncs per token; this cuts steady-state latency by ~15-25% in our tests for short seqs. the warmup path requires executing the graph for a representative sequence and batch shape. if you get a new shape we fallback to non-graph path and that can spike latency.
[04:12] Maya: is it feasible to maintain a small set of graphs to cover most of your workload?
[04:17] Arjun: yes, if your workload distribution is stable. we recommend creating graphs for the most common (batch, seq) pairs — e.g., (1,64), (4,64), (1,256). also we have an auto-graph manager that does lazy graph creation and TTL eviction, but there is a latency hit during first use.
[04:37] Ethan: any numbers for RTX 4090 vs A100?
[04:41] Arjun: ballpark: A100 has higher peak throughput and memory bandwidth so TRT-int8 fused kernels are ~1.6-1.9x faster than 4090 on big batches; but on small single-client latency critical loads 4090 with careful kernel selection and CUDA graphs can be comparable, ~0.9-1.1x depending on kernel. variance matters.
[05:05] Priya: interesting. what about quantization — we tried dynamic 8-bit and saw token quality drop for some prompts.
[05:13] Luis: quantization profiles matter — per-channel symmetric vs asymmetric, calibration dataset, and outlier handling. int8 with PTQ can reduce perf but needs calibration to avoid hallucination. TRT-LLM int8 is aggressive; vLLM + bitsandbytes 4-bit may be a safer middle ground.
[05:33] Sofia: ok let's talk about fallback policies. when TRT graph isn't available for a shape, do you degrade to vLLM or to non-graph TRT kernels?
[05:45] Arjun: our default is fallback to non-graph TRT kernel if model binary exists; if TRT path fails we have a policy to route to vLLM path on the same machine or another instance depending on latency/cost. can set per-tenant rules: strict-predictability (route to vLLM on dedicated machines) vs best-effort throughput.
[06:10] Maya: that routing is configurable in Redwood Dedicated and Private, correct?
[06:14] Arjun: yep, per-route config in the control plane.
[06:18] Sofia: what about measurement — how do you attribute latency to kernel selection vs memcpy vs CPU scheduling?
[06:24] Luis: we instrument per-kernel timings in the runtime with microsecond granularity and tag with a callstack: kernel_exec, memcpy_h2d, memcpy_d2h, cuda_graph_launch. we also collect host CPU queue time. combining those gives you a waterfall. recommended first step is run nvprof/NSIGHT and our in-runtime tracer to correlate.
[06:50] Ethan: can you share the profiling spreadsheet you referenced?
[06:52] Maya: yes Arjun has it — Arjun will share.
[06:55] Arjun: i'll put the kernel-selection perf spreadsheet in the shared drive after the call. it has A100/4090/RTX bench numbers across batch sizes and seq lengths.
[07:02] --- short pause, background noise ---
[07:10] Sofia: re: on-prem, we have SSO/SAML and KMS integrations needs — anything special for private deploy?
[07:18] Maya: Private (VPC/on-prem) supports KMS/HSM and you can disable outbound telemetry; we provide a control-plane shim and local agent. security docs will be shared.
[07:30] Priya: our ops worry: disk space and precompiled kernel binaries — TRT binaries can be hundreds of MBs per variant?
[07:38] Arjun: yes that is a real operational cost — storing tens of kernel variants per model can add up. tradeoff: fewer variants mean more runtime shape conversions and potential latency. we recommend pruning to top N variants per machine class.
[07:54] Ethan: any guidance on auto-batching? we see increased latency variance when auto-batching is on.
[07:59] Luis: auto-batching increases throughput by merging small requests but increases p95. tune the batching window and max_batch_size; for latency-sensitive services use small windows (e.g., 2-5 ms) and cap batch size. our optimize tool suggests settings based on traffic profile.
[08:22] Sofia: can we run a pilot where Redwood runs a 4-hour benchmark against our on-prem cluster? we will provide access windows.
[08:30] Maya: yes, we can. recommended scope: kernel-level microbenchmarks, full e2e throughput/latency tests, and a cuda-graph warmup pass.
[08:39] Arjun: for the microbenchmarks, we need representative prompts and seq distribution; also list of GPU types, driver versions, and cudnn/cuda versions.
[08:49] Sofia: we'll get that.
[08:52] Ethan: question — how do you handle multi-tenant noisy neighbor scenarios?
[08:57] Arjun: we have QoS via cgroups/nvlink isolation, and smart scheduling: route latency critical tenants to isolated queues; dedicated mode gives exclusive pools. also mem pinning for kv cache to reduce eviction thrash.
[09:15] Priya: what about NUMA effects on multi-GPU nodes?
[09:19] Luis: NUMA matters — binding host threads to the correct NUMA node and ensuring GPU peer access configs are set reduces cross-node memcpy. we add NUMA-aware allocator heuristics.
[09:32] Sofia: ok let's recap next steps quickly.
[09:36] Maya: recap: Arjun share spreadsheet + run microbenchmarks; Sofia to provide GPU inventory and prompts; Maya to share SOC2 and private deploy checklist; Luis to draft CUDA graph warmup runbook.
[09:50] Ethan: timeline — we can provide inventory by Friday (2026-11-13) and propose benchmark window 2026-11-16 02:00-06:00 local.
[10:00] Maya: sounds good. any blockers?
[10:05] Priya: just ops window approval, but should be fine.
[10:09] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and slack.
[10:12] End of recording.
